splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines or criminal statutes.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of defendants. This matters because it determines whether agencies can expand criminal liability through interpretive guidance rather than formal rulemaking.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over Auer/Kisor deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (Auer/Kisor) applies even in the criminal context, allowing the Sentencing Commission's interpretive commentary to control over the rule of lenity when Guidelines text is ambiguous.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and binding interpretation of the Guidelines text.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes such offenses. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders under the Guidelines.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and binding
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to deference, meaning inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary is invalid or non-binding
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that the commentary impermissibly expands the definition beyond the text, so conspiracy convictions do not qualify as career-offender predicates.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant must meet all three criminal-history disqualifiers listed in § 3553(f)(1) to be ineligible for safety-valve relief, or whether having any one is sufficient to disqualify. This split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on the circuit.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) are met.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that any single criminal-history criterion in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' or as distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines (U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b)) when the state-controlled substance is not listed on the federal schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled or whether any state-controlled substance qualifies. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-controlled substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the substance is federally scheduled, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) permitting such consideration is valid.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a non-retroactive change in law (specifically the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory stacked 25-year sentences for § 924(c) convictions) can support compassionate release. Some circuits hold it can never contribute to an extraordinary and compelling finding; others allow it. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment attempted to resolve this, but circuits dispute whether the Commission exceeded its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law, including the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment, may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must use habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241) rather than civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens) to challenge conditions of confinement that implicate the duration of custody, such as BOP decisions on earned time credits under the First Step Act.
splits.description: Circuits have developed an unresolved longstanding split on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging BOP decisions that affect the duration or terms of confinement (such as denial of earned time credits), or whether civil rights actions are also available. The Supreme Court left this question open in Preiser v. Rodriguez and has not resolved it.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-of-confinement challenges
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges decisions affecting the fact or duration of confinement, including BOP credit determinations, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights claims (such as Bivens or § 1983 actions) to challenge certain conditions of confinement even when those conditions implicate the duration of custody, and habeas is not the sole remedy.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted in good faith to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between filing a Chapter 13 petition and converting to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held such appreciation belongs to the estate based on the broad scope of § 541(a), while other circuits have held the opposite, finding that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects debtors from losing post-petition appreciation upon good-faith conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) was designed to protect good-faith converting debtors, and post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation remains with the debtor rather than becoming part of the converted Chapter 7 estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the deadline to appeal a Hyde Amendment order (for attorney's fees in criminal cases) is governed by the civil appeal timeline (60 days under FRAP 4(a)) or the criminal appeal timeline (14 days under FRAP 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though arising from a criminal case, is a civil matter for appeal-timing purposes. The answer determines whether a defendant has 14 or 60 days to file a notice of appeal, with significant practical consequences for litigants.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 60-day civil appeal deadline applies when the government is a party.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case and thus the 14-day criminal appeal deadline governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly consider punishment as a purpose of supervised release revocation sentences, or whether supervised release revocation must be limited to rehabilitative and public-safety goals.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether punishment is a permissible purpose when sentencing a defendant upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts expressly to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split where other circuits limit revocation sentences to deterrence, rehabilitation, and public safety.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose punishment for violations of supervised release at revocation, not limited solely to rehabilitation or public safety goals.

positions.label: Punishment is not a proper purpose
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sentences should focus on rehabilitation, deterrence, and public safety, not retributive punishment for the violation itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan be fixed as of the end of the prior plan year, or whether the actuary retains discretion to select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the statutory measurement date requires all actuarial assumptions to be determined as of the end of the prior plan year, providing employers with greater predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Actuary may select assumptions after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary retains discretion to select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans to use the most current and accurate data available.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the term specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, so the clock pauses and the court retains jurisdiction to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: No tolling — term runs continuously
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release terms run continuously regardless of absconding, and courts lack authority to apply a judicially-created tolling doctrine without explicit statutory authorization.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits raising any claim previously presented — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended, in addition to § 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim that was previously raised in a prior collateral attack.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar does not apply to federal prisoners under § 2255, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to election rules. The question implicates whether courts can evaluate ballot-counting procedures before harm materializes or whether such challenges must wait until after an election, with significant consequences for the administrability of election law litigation.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when a state law changes the rules governing ballot counting, even before an election occurs.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's alleged injury from post-Election Day ballot counting is too speculative to confer Article III standing for a pre-election challenge.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal court documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether denial of a motion to seal medical records constitutes a collateral order that is effectively unreviewable on appeal from a final judgment. The D.C. Circuit held that privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review, while some other circuits have reached different conclusions about whether such orders meet the collateral order criteria.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that would be irreparably lost without immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders, even those involving medical records, do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because they can be adequately vindicated through other means or on appeal after final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve differing approaches among the circuits regarding the standards for liability and remedies in discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators. The Second Circuit's approach was found sufficiently unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a circuit split on applicable standards.

positions.label: Second Circuit's approach
positions.summary: Applied its own standards regarding discrimination claims in hospitality settings, which SCOTUS found warranted review as potentially inconsistent with other circuits' approaches.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different or more refined standards for evaluating discrimination liability and damages in hospitality and business establishment cases.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
